narrative:
The model predicted an 86.7% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess long-term success in law school, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, both pushing the prediction strongly toward failure. You placed in the bottom decile for grades in both Year 1 and Year 3, compared with an average around the middle of the class (roughly 6th and 5.8th decile) among students who were accepted. These unusually low academic standings in law school were the main reasons the model saw high risk of bar exam failure.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure. At 28, it sits well below the average of 37 among accepted students, signaling weaker preparation in the eyes of the model.

Your undergraduate GPA of 2.5 (versus an accepted average of 3.23), middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and were not decisive.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your class rank through targeted academic support and consider retaking the LSAT to boost your score. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
